title: Little Paris, Then the Bulldozers: Seven Days in Bucharest

bestPeriod.window: mid-May to mid-June and the whole of September, terrace weather without the 38 °C concrete oven
bestPeriod.avoid: mid-July to late August (heat, and half the good kitchens close for the month)

food.note: €175, €315 (€25, €45/day, Bucharest is still startlingly cheap for the quality)

transport.note: €25, €60 (metro and surface passes, one airport bus, two day-trip transfers)

activities.note: €90, €170 (Palace of Parliament, Primăverii, Village Museum, Therme)

hook: Bucharest does not tidy itself up for you. A Brâncovenesc monastery church sits in a hole below street level with an office block on top of it; a 1930s Modernist apartment slab by a Dada founder faces a boulevard that ate a whole neighbourhood. Seven days here is not padding, it is the minimum needed to walk the belle-époque villas, the interwar concrete, the Ceaușescu Civic Centre and the parks, and to eat properly while doing it.

snapshot.Getting there: Henri Coandă (OTP), 17 km north. **Express bus 783** runs OTP → Piața Unirii via Piața Victoriei roughly every 20-30 min, ~40-60 min; buy the card at the STB kiosk in the arrivals hall before boarding. Rail links to Gara de Nord also run from the airport halt.

itinerary.title: Centrul Vechi, at ground level
itinerary.morning: Bus 783 in, drop bags, and walk straight into **Lipscani**. Start at **Stavropoleos monastery** (1724), the finest Brâncovenesc stone carving in the city, a courtyard of salvaged tombstones, and total silence forty metres from the bar strip.
itinerary.afternoon: **Hanul lui Manuc**, the 1808 merchants' caravanserai, still built around its wooden-galleried courtyard. Then the ruins of the **Curtea Veche**, Vlad Țepeș's princely court, and the Old Princely Court church, the oldest in Bucharest.
itinerary.evening: **Caru' cu Bere** on Str. Stavropoleos, 1899, neo-Gothic vaults, stained glass, and yes it is touristed, and yes the *mici* and the house beer are still correct. Book, or queue.

itinerary.title: Calea Victoriei, end to end
itinerary.morning: From Piața Victoriei walk south. The **Romanian Athenaeum** (1888, Albert Galleron), go inside; the circular fresco of Romanian history runs the full drum. Then the **Revolution Square** ensemble: the former **Central Committee** building and **the balcony** from which Ceaușescu addressed the crowd on 21 December 1989 and heard it turn on him.
itinerary.afternoon: South past the **CEC Palace** (1900, Paul Gottereau) with its glass dome, into **Cărturești Carusel**, a bookshop in a gutted 19th-century Chrissoveloni bank, six white floors of light.
itinerary.evening: **Lacrimi și Sfinți** on Str. Șepcari, Romanian ingredients, unfussy, a menu that changes on what came in. One of the few places doing serious regional cooking without folklore.

itinerary.title: The Civic Centre and what it replaced
itinerary.morning: **Palace of Parliament** tour, booked, ID in hand. The second-largest administrative building on earth by floor area after the Pentagon, 1,100 rooms, and a marble bill that beggared the country. The guide will give you the numbers; the roof terrace gives you the view down Bd. Unirii.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the boulevard east, then hunt the buried churches: **Schitul Maicilor** and **Mihai Vodă**, both moved on rails in the 1980s and now boxed behind apartment blocks. This half-day is the point of the trip.
itinerary.evening: Metro M2 south to **Bellu cemetery** if the light holds, Romania's Père-Lachaise, with Eminescu, Caragiale and Enescu, and funerary sculpture worth an hour. Then dinner at **Hanu' Berarilor**, in one of its restored 19th-century houses.

itinerary.title: Cotroceni, and the two great museums
itinerary.morning: **Cotroceni Palace**, the royal residence turned presidential complex; the museum wing is visited **by advance-booked guided tour with ID**, same rule as the Parliament. Then walk the surrounding streets: Dr. Lister, Dr. Clunet, the Neo-Romanian villa stock at its densest.
itinerary.afternoon: North to Piața Victoriei for the **Muzeul Țăranului Român** (Romanian Peasant Museum), textiles, icons on glass, and a whole wooden church reassembled inside. It is a design object as much as an ethnographic one.
itinerary.evening: Next door, **Grigore Antipa** natural history museum stays open late enough on some days to combine. Dinner at **Zexe Zahana**, Bucharest's argument for its own historic recipes, cooked from archive menus.

itinerary.title: Armenească, Mântuleasa and the quiet streets
itinerary.morning: **Armenească**: the Armenian church of 1911, the low 19th-century houses, and the best-preserved fabric of pre-war residential Bucharest. Slow, flat, almost no traffic.
itinerary.afternoon: **Mântuleasa**, the street Mircea Eliade made into a novella, plus the **Foișorul de Foc** fire tower and Grădina Icoanei. Hunt Marcel Iancu's Modernist houses on Str. Negustori and around Dorobanți; several are marked.
itinerary.evening: **Kane** in the Dorobanți grid, tasting-menu cooking with Romanian produce, one of the city's best kitchens. Book a week out. Afterwards, **Nomad Skybar** in the old town for the rooftop, which is the only way to see the Civic Centre's scale at night.

itinerary.title: Out of town: Mogoșoaia and Snagov
itinerary.morning: **Mogoșoaia Palace**, 14 km north-west, built 1698-1702 by Constantin Brâncoveanu and the definitional example of the style named after him, loggia, carved stone, a lake behind. Forty minutes by car, or bus from Laromet.
itinerary.afternoon: **Snagov**, the lake and the island monastery reached by boat, where tradition (not evidence) puts the grave of Vlad Țepeș. It is a genuinely peaceful afternoon and the woodland around the lake is the closest real forest to the city.
itinerary.evening: Back for something simple in the centre: *ciorbă*, *tochitură*, a glass of Fetească Neagră.

itinerary.title: Primăverii, the park, and the water
itinerary.morning: **Primăverii Palace** on Bd. Primăverii, the Ceaușescu family villa, opened to visitors in 2016 and left as it was: the peacock mosaics, the indoor pool, Elena's wardrobes. Timed tickets, book ahead.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk into **Herăstrău / Regele Mihai I park** and along the lake to the **Muzeul Satului (Village Museum)**, 300-odd relocated rural buildings from every Romanian region on 100 open-air hectares, one of the oldest such museums in Europe (founded 1936).
itinerary.evening: If your flight is late, **Therme București** at Balotești sits between the city and the airport, Europe's largest thermal water complex, palm houses, slides and quiet pools, with a shuttle from Piața Presei. Shower, change, and go straight to OTP.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Cișmigiu
accommodationStrategy.description: a 1912 building on the edge of Cișmigiu gardens, two minutes from the M1/M3 Izvor and Universitate axis, and walking distance to both the old town and the Civic Centre, the two poles of this itinerary.
accommodationStrategy.booking: online, 3-4 weeks ahead; ask for a room off the boulevard, which is loud.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rembrandt Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: inside the old town but on the quieter northern edge, so you get Lipscani on foot without the 03:00 bar noise. Small, long-established, and the staff genuinely know the restaurant scene.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct, 4-6 weeks ahead, it has few rooms and fills.

accommodationStrategy.name: Epoque Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: the quietest good hotel in the centre, with a pool and a parking option that matters if you hire a car for the Mogoșoaia and Snagov day. Ten minutes' walk to Calea Victoriei.

logistics.connectivity: 5G across the whole city and free Wi-Fi on much of the metro and in cafés. Romanian mobile data is among the fastest and cheapest in the EU; a local eSIM is barely worth the trouble for a week if you have EU roaming.
logistics.emergency: **112**, English answered. Pharmacies marked *farmacie*; several near Piața Romană are 24-hour.
logistics.weather: Bucharest sits on a plain with no relief, July and August routinely exceed 35 °C and the concrete holds it overnight. May and September are the reason to come. Sudden violent thunderstorms in late spring flood underpasses; give the metro an extra fifteen minutes.
logistics.bookingWindows: Palace of Parliament 5-10 days (weekends longer). Primăverii Palace 3-7 days. Kane a week. Caru' cu Bere for dinner, 2-3 days. Everything else walk-in.
logistics.money: Romanian **leu (RON)**; €1 ≈ 5.10-5.25 RON. Cards are accepted almost everywhere including buses and markets; keep 100-150 RON cash for church donations, small markets and the Snagov boatman. Romania is in the EU but **not** the euro, do not assume euro acceptance.
logistics.transportRules: Validate or tap on entry to every STB vehicle; inspectors are active on the trams. Metro runs roughly 05:00-23:00. If you hire a car for the day trips, a **rovinietă** e-vignette is compulsory on national roads outside the city: category A costs **€3.50 (~18 RON)** for one day or **€6 (~31 RON)** for ten days, there is no seven-day product. Buy it at any fuel station or online before you drive.
logistics.permits: No permits. Photo ID is a hard requirement for Parliament and Cotroceni. Photography is restricted in parts of the Parliament and forbidden in Primăverii's private rooms; drone flying over the Civic Centre is prohibited.

proTips: Book the Palace of Parliament for **09:00 or 09:30**, the first slot. Groups arrive from 11:00, the rooms echo, and the early tour moves at half the pace.
Carry your passport every day, not a photocopy. Two of the best visits in this file, Parliament and Cotroceni, refuse entry on a photocopy or a phone photo.
Use the metro north-south (M2) and walk east-west. The M2 crosses the whole city in 20 minutes; the surface equivalent at rush hour is an hour.
Go to Bellu cemetery at 16:00 on a weekday. Low light, empty avenues, and the sculpture reads properly, it is the one place in Bucharest that rewards being slow.
Order *ciorbă de burtă* once and *ciorbă rădăuțeană* once, and decide. The first is tripe and garlic and sour cream; the second is chicken, gentler, and the one to start with.
Ask at any old-town bar for a *palincă* rather than a vodka. The Transylvanian double-distilled plum spirit runs 40-55% and is the house drink that locals actually order.
Do Therme on the way to the airport, not as a day trip. It is 20 minutes from OTP and 45 from the centre, the geography only works one way.

raw.Walkable neighbourhood blocks: **Centrul Vechi** (Lipscani, Str. Franceză, Hanul lui Manuc, Stavropoleos), dense, flat, one hour end to end. **Calea Victoriei**, the spine, 2.7 km from Piața Victoriei to Splaiul Independenței, walkable in a morning with stops. **Cotroceni**, a grid of belle-époque and Neo-Romanian villas around the palace and the Botanical Garden, best on foot for two hours. **Dorobanți / Primăverii**, leafy, embassy-heavy, low-rise; the Ceaușescu family villa sits in it. **Armenească and Mântuleasa**, the two quietest historic quarters in the centre, half-restored, entirely residential. **Uranus / Casa Poporului**, not walkable in the ordinary sense; the Civic Centre was built at a scale that defeats pedestrians, and you cross it deliberately. **Herăstrău / Regele Mihai I**, the big northern park, 3 km of lakeside path.
raw.Transit passes and fares: The metro is run by **Metrorex** (lines **M1** circle-ish, **M2** north-south, **M3** west, **M4** north-west, **M5** Drumul Taberei); the buses, trams and trolleybuses are **STB**. They use different ticketing: STB sells the reloadable **Multiplu**/Activ card, metro sells its own card or contactless bank-card entry at the gates. Rough figures: STB single trip ~3 RON (€0.60), 24-hour ~10 RON, weekly ~20 RON; metro 2-trip ~6 RON, 10-trip ~25 RON, 24-hour ~10 RON, weekly ~30 RON; bus 783 to the airport carries a supplement over the standard fare. Contactless bank-card tap-in works on both networks and is the simplest option for a week.
raw.The honest transport note: Bucharest traffic is genuinely severe, among the worst-congested cities in Europe, and a 6 km taxi at 18:00 can take 45 minutes. **The metro plus walking beats taxis** for almost every itinerary in this file. Use Bolt or Uber for late nights and the two day trips only.
raw.Cultural booking timelines: The **Palace of Parliament** is the binding one: tours must be **booked in advance online** and you must carry a **passport or national ID card** matching the booking, checked at the entrance. Turn up without it and you are refused, no exceptions. Book 5-10 days ahead in season, longer for weekends; the standard tour runs ~45-75 minutes and costs around 60-70 RON. The **Primăverii Palace** (Ceaușescu's residence) sells timed slots and sells out days ahead in summer. Everything else, Antipa, the Peasant Museum, the Village Museum, is same-day.
raw.Architectural focal points, with periods: **Brâncovenesc** (late 17th-early 18th c.): Stavropoleos monastery church, Kretzulescu church, Antim monastery, carved stone, twisted colonnettes, deep porches. **Neo-Romanian** (from c. 1886): the national style invented by **Ion Mincu**, who fused Brâncovenesc detail with Beaux-Arts planning, Casa Vernescu and the Central School for Girls are his; the style saturates Cotroceni. **Interwar Bucharest Modernism** (1929-1940): **Horia Creangă**'s ARO Building on Bd. Magheru (now Cinema Patria), a landmark of European Modernism, and **Marcel Iancu**, who co-founded **Dada** at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916 before returning to Bucharest to build some thirty houses, then emigrating to Palestine in 1941. **Socialist Civic Centre** (1980s): Bd. Unirii and the Palace of Parliament, designed under **Anca Petrescu**.
raw.Systematisation, what was destroyed: After the 1977 earthquake, Ceaușescu's *sistematizare* programme levelled roughly a fifth of the historic centre to build the Civic Centre: the Uranus and Antim quarters, some 40,000 people displaced, and around **two dozen churches** demolished or hidden. Several were physically **moved on rails**, Schitul Maicilor and the Mihai Vodă church were rolled hundreds of metres and walled in behind blocks, where they still stand, invisible from the street. Look for them; they are the best argument this city makes.
